summary: A humorous April Fools memo describing a protocol suite for an infinite number of monkeys at typewriters, who try to type the works of Shakespeare or a good television show. It is not a real working protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2795 is an April 1st joke about an infinite number of monkeys typing at typewriters. It invents a protocol suite for checking their status, supplying resources, collecting their text, and deciding whether the text matches Shakespeare or is original.

subtitle: An April 1st joke that specifies protocols for managing an infinite number of typing monkeys.

tldr.problem: This April 1st joke treats the infinite-monkey thought experiment as an engineering task: collect transcripts, maintain the monkeys, and decide whether their writing matches a classic work or is new.
tldr.mechanism: The fictional IMPS suite connects monkey interfaces to organizations and transcript reviewers using KEEPER, CHIMP, IAMB-PENT, and PAN.
tldr.outcome: The memo is an Informational joke RFC. It presents a detailed mock protocol suite rather than a real system to implement.

today: RFC 2795 is an Informational April 1st RFC, and the unit metadata lists no RFC as obsoleting or updating it. It presents a fictional protocol suite as a joke, not a real system to deploy.

sections.title: An April 1st Joke About Monkey Transcripts
sections.content:
RFC 2795 is dated 1 April 2000 and is an April 1st joke document. It treats the idea that infinitely many monkeys at infinitely many typewriters might produce Shakespeare as an engineering problem. The memo asks how anyone would collect the text, identify a match, and provide for the monkeys' basic needs.

The Infinite Monkey Protocol Suite (IMPS) is presented as an experimental set of protocols for collecting, transferring, and reviewing transcripts. The joke is delivered through detailed packet formats, command names, and example exchanges.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an April 1st joke written as a protocol specification. It imagines how a network might manage typing monkeys and review what they produce.

sections.title: The IMPS Participants and Packet Format
sections.content:
The memo defines four main kinds of participant. ZOOs maintain groups of monkeys and their equipment. A SIMIAN is an interface attached to an individual monkey that sends status reports and resource requests to a ZOO. A BARD checks transcripts against published works, while a CRITIC reviews new work for possible publication.

IMPS packets identify a version, sequence number, protocol number, reserved field, size, source, destination, and data. Source and destination use the memo's Infinite TAG identifier encoding. The memo presents the format as a universal protocol structure for the fictional suite.
sections.plainLanguage: A ZOO manages the monkeys, and a SIMIAN interface communicates with it. BARDs check for matches with existing works, while CRITICs review new transcripts.

sections.title: Managing Monkeys and Sending Their Text
sections.content:
KEEPER is a connectionless protocol through which a ZOO sends a request to a SIMIAN in one packet and receives a response in another. Its requests include STATUS, HEARTBEAT, WAKEUP, TYPE, FASTER, TRANSCRIPT, and STOP. Responses include status codes such as ASLEEP, DISTRACTED, ALIVE, and DEAD, as well as ACCEPT and REFUSE.

CHIMP is connection-oriented. A SIMIAN can request resources such as food, water, medicine, a veterinarian, or a technician; request replacement or cleaning of equipment; notify the ZOO of a status; and send a transcript. The ZOO responds with messages such as ACCEPT, DELAY, REFUSE, or RECEIVED. The RFC supplies an example exchange involving a monkey named BoBo.
sections.plainLanguage: KEEPER carries short control requests and status replies. CHIMP carries longer conversations, including requests for supplies and the text typed by a monkey.

sections.title: Checking and Reviewing Transcripts
sections.content:
A ZOO uses IAMB-PENT to send a transcript to a BARD for comparison with existing works. The BARD can report that it found or did not find the work in its collection. The command names and required response forms use Shakespearean-style words and syllable patterns.

A ZOO uses PAN to send a transcript to a CRITIC for review as a potentially new work. PAN includes responses such as IMPRESS_ME and REJECT, with rejection codes that give reasons in the memo's satirical style. The security section continues the joke while naming risks such as spoofing, denial of service, and cleartext transmissions.
sections.plainLanguage: IAMB-PENT asks whether a transcript matches a work already in the BARD's collection. PAN sends new text to a CRITIC, which can reject it with one of the memo's humorous reasons.
